bib.title: Character-level Convolutional Networks for Text Classification

question: Can a deep 1-D convolutional network applied to raw characters, with no word knowledge, classify text as well as word-based and n-gram models?
hypothesis: Deep character-level ConvNets do not need words and can reach competitive or state-of-the-art accuracy when trained on large-scale datasets.
contributions: First application of ConvNets only on characters
Eight new large-scale text classification datasets (hundreds of thousands to millions of samples)
Comparison against bag-of-words, n-grams, TFIDF, bag-of-means, word-based ConvNets and LSTM

method.summary: A 9-layer (6 conv, 3 fully-connected) temporal ConvNet reads 1014 one-hot characters from a 70-symbol alphabet and is trained with SGD from scratch per dataset. Compared on eight datasets against linear models on hand-built features, word2vec bag-of-means, word-based ConvNets and a word LSTM.

datasets.name: Sogou News
datasets.source: SogouCA + SogouCS, 2,909,551 articles; labelled by URL domain
datasets.preprocessing: Chinese converted to Pinyin with pypinyin + jieba segmentation so English models apply unchanged; title and content

datasets.name: Yahoo! Answers
datasets.source: Yahoo! Webscope Comprehensive Q&A v1.0, 4,483,032 questions
datasets.preprocessing: question title, question content, best answer

models.name: Large char ConvNet
models.architecture: 6 conv (1024 features; kernels 7,7,3,3,3,3; pools 3,3,N/A,N/A,N/A,3; stride 1) + FC 2048, 2048, output = classes; ReLU; 2 dropout 0.5
models.init_from: Gaussian init, mean 0 std 0.02; trained from scratch
models.tokenizer: none; one-hot characters, alphabet 70 (26 letters, 10 digits, 33 other, newline); unknown chars all-zero

models.name: Small char ConvNet
models.architecture: as Large but 256 conv features and FC 1024, 1024

models.name: Full-alphabet ConvNet
models.architecture: same, alphabet distinguishes upper and lower case
models.vocab: inferred: 70 plus 26 upper-case letters (size not stated)

models.name: Word-based ConvNet (word2vec or lookup table)
models.architecture: same layer count and sizes as char ConvNets
models.init_from: pretrained word2vec (Mikolov 2013) or end-to-end lookup table

models.name: LSTM
models.architecture: vanilla word-based LSTM, mean of outputs, multinomial logistic regression

training.objective: inferred: cross-entropy classification (multinomial logistic output); not named
training.epochs: inferred: 30 (halved every 3 epochs for 10 times); not stated directly
training.hardware: 2 Tesla K40 GPUs (donated by NVIDIA); AWS grant

other.epoch_size_minibatches: 5,000 (AG, Sogou, DBPedia, Yelp P/F); 10,000 (Yahoo); 30,000 (Amazon F/P); each epoch a fixed number of random samples uniformly across classes
other.augmentation: WordNet-derived LibreOffice mytheas thesaurus; r replaced words with P[r]~p^r, synonym index P[s]~q^s, p=0.5, q=0.5
other.character_order: quantised in backward order so latest characters sit near the beginning; characters beyond 1014 ignored

baselines: BoW (50,000 most frequent words, multinomial logistic regression)
Bag-of-ngrams (500,000 most frequent n-grams up to 5)
Bag-of-means (k-means, 5000 means, word2vec dim 300, words seen >5 times)
eval.protocol: Single reported test error per cell; no seeds, no confidence intervals; 'reported faithfully without any model selection'

evidence.quote: initial step size 0.01 which is halved every 3 epoches for 10 times

results.claim: The pooling module let them train ConvNets deeper than 6 layers, where others failed.

limits: Authors say their experiments show no explicit evidence that ConvNets handle misspellings and emoticons better; hypothesis needs further analysis.
Case-sensitivity regularisation explanation is 'to be validated'.
Bag-of-means conclusion does not speak for other uses of word2vec.
Only classification; structured output left to future work.
Single run per cell, no variance reported; parameter count and training time not given.
Sogou handled via Pinyin, so 'characters' there are romanised letters, not Chinese characters.
Predates subword tokenisation (BPE) and transformers; fixed 1014-character window.

terms.definition: prescribing an alphabet of size m and quantizing each character as a one-hot vector; out-of-alphabet characters are all-zero vectors
